extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy, aesthetics, and civic education (readers of Plato)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging whether poetic/imitative art is fit to educate citizens and belong in a well-ordered State — focusing on truth, emotional effects, usefulness, and conformity with reason and law. Drawn from Plato's arguments about poets, imitation, and the harms/benefits of poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not awaken or nourish irrational parts of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: The imitative poet awakens, nourishes, and strengthens the irrational feelings (pity, rage, lust, etc.) and thereby impairs reason; because these affections have no discernment of greater or less, they are unfit to rule in the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato argues that poetry which stimulates the passions rather than fostering reason should be excluded from a well-ordered State. Examples given: theatrical passages that excite long lamentations or weeping, comic jests that one would be ashamed to utter oneself, and scenes that stimulate lust or anger. Anti-pattern: praising or popularizing passions that citizens would otherwise restrain as disgraceful in themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry must not manufacture false images far removed from truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet is compared to the painter as a manufacturer of images whose creations possess an inferior degree of truth and concern an inferior part of the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because imitative art represents appearances rather than reality, it risks misleading the soul. The text uses the analogy of the painter and asserts that poetry, being twice removed from truth (appearance of appearance), should not be taken as a serious educator. The implication for evaluation: prefer works aligned with truth and reason over mere semblance or flattering images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid art that trains people to take pleasure in what they would abominate in themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectators may delight in sympathetic indulgence of pity or laughter at another's misfortunes or indecencies, while condemning those very reactions in themselves; poetry that encourages this hypocrisy spreads evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato illustrates how people enjoy the recitation of a pitiful hero's lament yet would consider weeping shameful when it is their own misfortune. Similarly, jests on stage provoke laughter for things an individual would not make himself. Evaluation should therefore flag works that normalize conduct the audience would otherwise reject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should not encourage imitation of passionate, fitful temper
rubrics_metrics.description: The popular imitative poet prefers the passionate and fitful temper because it is easily imitated and pleases a promiscuous crowd; such temper is unsuitable for educating the rational principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In judging poetry intended for public consumption, beware works that glorify volatility, uncontrolled emotion, or spectacle. A civic standard favors representations that model steadiness, reason, and the 'wise and calm temperament' — traits 'not easy to imitate' but necessary for a well-ordered polis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit only poetry that is useful to the State and human life
rubrics_metrics.description: Only those poems which can be shown to be both pleasant and useful to States and human life ought to be admitted; specifically Plato proposes hymns to the gods and praises of famous men as acceptable forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explicitly states: 'hymns to the gods and praises of famous men are the only poetry which ought to be admitted into our State.' It permits defenders of poetry to make a case (in metre or in prose) proving that poetry is not merely delightful but beneficial to civic education. Usefulness to the State and moral improvement are the test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate poetry by law and reason rather than by pleasure and pain
rubrics_metrics.description: If the honeyed muse is allowed (epic or lyric), pleasure and pain rather than law and the reason of mankind will rule in the State; therefore law/reason must constrain poetic influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should judge whether poetic works place pleasure/pain above law and rational order. If so, they are politically and morally dangerous. The recommended policy is regulation or exclusion to prevent poetry from making passion the ruler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require poets to defend their art's civic value
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should be allowed to return from exile only if it can 'make a defence of herself' by proving usefulness; defenders may speak in lyrical or prose terms to show poetry's salutary effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural/epistemic criterion: allow poetry provisionally only on demonstration of concrete benefits to human life and the State. In practice, this means demanding explicit arguments or evidence that a poetic form cultivates virtue, wisdom, or appropriate emotional responses rather than corrupting them.
